unit.title: Managing your portfolio
unit.description: Rebalance, keep an eye on costs, invest little by little, measure properly and write your plan

texts: A 60/40 that goes back into shape
Real data from 2000 to 2012, with two big stock market falls. Your portfolio is **60 % shares and 40 % bonds**, and every January **you go back to that split**: you rebalance.
US shares (S&P 500)
US bonds
Emerging-market shares
If you'd never touched it, how much of your 60/40 would be in shares by 2012?
About 60 %
More than 80 %
Less than 50 %
In those years bonds rose far more than shares: left alone, it ended up **47 % in shares**. It was no longer the portfolio you chose.
Find a rebalanced mix whose worst fall doesn't go beyond 20 %.
Rebalancing keeps **the risk you chose**. And this time it also added something: selling expensive bonds to buy cheap shares left €17,073 versus €16,373 left alone.
Lots of stock market: even if you rebalance, the fall is big.
That's it! Fewer shares, smaller falls.
Move the mix and look at the worst fall
Time to rebalance?
Your plan: **60 % shares and 40 % bonds**. You correct it if one part drifts **more than 5 points**. What do you do in each case?
Move from shares to bonds
Move from bonds to shares
Leave it alone
After two good years you're at 72/28
12 points too many in shares: sell a little or add to bonds.
March 2020: the market crashes and you're at 50/50
It's scary, but your rule says buy shares: you're buying cheap.
You're at 62/38
Only 2 points: within your margin.
The market shoots up and you're at 68/32
8 points too many: back to 60/40.
After a sharp fall you're at 53/47
7 points short in shares: time to top up.
You're at 57/43
3 points: no need to touch anything.
Decide all six cases.
Rebalancing makes you **sell some of what rose most and buy what fell behind**, without guessing anything. In a crash it's scary; that's why it's worth having the rule written down.
Look at how many points it has drifted from 60 %: more than 5?
What do you do in each case?

steps.title: Three ways to rebalance
steps.body:
1. **By calendar:** once a year, for example in January.
2. **By threshold:** when one part drifts more than 5 points.
3. **With contributions:** new money goes to whatever has fallen short. You don't sell, so you don't trigger any tax.

With investment funds you can also rebalance through a **fund transfer** (a Spanish «traspaso»), without paying tax.
steps.key: Calendar, threshold or contributions: what matters is having a rule and sticking to it.
steps.tip: Try it: in Portfolio, check the «Portfolio weight» of each asset against your plan.

texts: «Commission: €0»
Irene
I've bought €1,000 of an ETF that trades in **dollars**. Purchase commission: €0. Free!
There's another line on the statement: «Currency conversion: 0.5 %».
What did the purchase really cost her?
Nothing: the commission was €0
The purchase commission, yes. But converting her euros to dollars took **€5**.
€5 now, and another conversion the day she sells
That's it: you pay the conversion going in and coming out. Round trip, 1 % of what you invested.
€5 every year
It isn't yearly: you pay it each time euros are converted to dollars, when buying and when selling.
And how do I avoid it?
Many indices have an ETF that **trades in euros**: buy that one and there's no conversion to pay.
Check **custody** too: some brokers charge a fee for holding your securities, whether you trade or not.
The cost nobody invoices

You start with €1,000 and add **€150 a month** for 25 years, with the market at 6 % a year (an example, not a promise). **Ongoing charges** never arrive on an invoice: they're taken out of the fund's value. One fund charges **0.2 %**; the other, **1.2 %**.
Over 25 years, how much does that extra point a year take?
About €1,400
About €14,000
About €46,000
With the cheap one you end up with **€102,639**; with the expensive one, **€88,629**. That point takes €14,010, and €46,000 came out of your pocket.
Stretch the period to 40 years and look at the gap.
Ongoing charges are **already subtracted** from the return you see: they don't show on your statement. You have to look for the figure in the fund's document, the **KID**.
More than €60,000 over 40 years. And no invoice ever arrived.
The longer the period, the more each tenth of a point weighs.
Move the years and the expensive fund's fee

steps.title: The KID cost table
steps.body:
The key information document (**KID**) includes the table «Composition of costs»:

• **Entry and exit costs**: when you buy and when you sell.
• **Ongoing costs**: management and expenses, every year.
• **Transaction costs**: what the fund spends buying and selling its holdings.
• **Performance fees**: only in some funds.

On top of that comes what your broker charges: commission per trade, custody and currency conversion.
steps.key: Add up the product's costs (KID) and your broker's: what counts is the total for each year.
steps.tip: Try it: ask Lumi where to find an ETF's KID.

u30l3.title: Investing with a little: €50 a month

texts: €3 out of every €50
Dani
I already put **€50 a month** into a global ETF. My broker charges **€3** per purchase. That's not much, is it?
What share of each contribution goes on commission?
0.6 %: almost nothing
Do the sum: 3 ÷ 50 = 0.06. That's **6 %**, ten times more.
6 %: every contribution starts off losing
That's it. Out of every €50, only €47 actually gets invested.
It doesn't matter: what counts is contributing
Contributing matters, yes. But 6 % less every month, for years, is a lot of money.
What if I save up three months and buy €150 in one go?
Then you pay €3 on €150: **2 %**. Bundling contributions reduces the weight of a fixed commission.
Better still: a regular savings plan with **no commission per purchase**.
The leaks in your contribution
You put in **€50 a month**: €600 a year. These fixed costs are charged the same whether you put in €50 or €5,000. Switch off the ones you could avoid by changing broker.
Commission per purchase
Custody
Account maintenance
A €3 commission on each monthly purchase. What share of your €600 a year does it take?
3 × 12 = **€36 a year**: 6 % of what you contribute. With custody and maintenance it's €78: 13 %.
Switch off all three fixed costs.

That €78 a year, invested for 30 years at 7 % (an example, not a promise), would be **€7,601**: more than twelve years of your contributions. With little money, **the first thing is to pay no fixed costs**.
Zero fixed costs! Now your whole €50 goes to work.
Good. And the others?
Switch off each cost and see what it adds up to per year

steps.title: Investing with little, without leaks
steps.body:
• **No commission per purchase**: look for a free regular savings plan.
• **No custody or maintenance fees.**
• **No minimum amount**, or a low one.
• **Automatic**: on the day you get paid.

If your broker charges a fixed commission, bundle several contributions into a single purchase.
steps.key: With little money, a fixed cost weighs far more than a tenth of a point in annual fees.
steps.tip: Try it: in Market, buy €50 of a global ETF, such as VWCE, with your virtual money.

texts: The fund made money; Laura didn't
Laura
Laura puts €1,000 into a fund. It rises 20 %: she now has €1,200.
It's doing great! I'll put in another €10,000.
Right after that, the fund falls 10 %. Laura has €10,080.
Has Laura made money or lost it?
She's made money: the fund is up 8 % overall
The fund has, yes. But Laura put in €11,000 and has €10,080.
She's lost €920, even though the fund is up 8 %
Exactly! She had almost everything in just as it fell.
She's lost 10 %, like the fund
The fund doesn't lose overall: it's up 8 %. And she loses €920.
**Time**-weighted: what the fund did. Used to compare funds.
**Money**-weighted: what **you** made, depending on when you put your money in.
How much is that a year?
A fund turns **€10,000 into €15,000** in 5 years: +50 % in total. What yearly pace is that?
+50 % in 5 years: how much is that a year?
10 % a year: 50 divided by 5
A bit less than 10 % a year
50 % a year
Interest compounds: at 10 % a year, €10,000 would become **€16,105** in 5 years. You need less.
Find the annual % that turns €10,000 into about €15,000 in 5 years.
+50 % in 5 years is **8.4 % a year**, not 10 %: annualising is compounding in reverse. Always compare **% a year with % a year**.
Too high: each year's interest earns interest too.
Spot on! Neither 10 % nor 50 %: just over 8 %.
Move the annual % until you reach €15,000

steps.title: Measuring honestly
steps.body:
Subtract fees and taxes, compare with a benchmark index and remember inflation.

An app telling you «+40 % since you started» without saying over how many years tells you almost nothing.
steps.key: To compare, use the annualised return; to know how much you made, use the money-weighted one.
steps.tip: Try it: compare your Portfolio's «Return» with that of SXR8, an S&P 500 ETF, over the same time.

texts: Your plan, on one page
Ana
In March 2020 the stock market fell 30 % and I sold everything.
Then it went up and I was left out. How do I stop it happening again?
With a written plan on one page: your **Investment Policy Statement**.
It says what you do, why, and what you'll do when the market turns ugly.
Point 8: «If the market falls 30 %, I…»
…sell everything and come back when it calms down
You don't decide that calmly: fear decides it for you.
…don't sell, keep investing and rebalance if needed
That's a plan! And rebalancing will make you buy cheap.
…will see what the news says
In the middle of a panic, the news won't tell you where the bottom is. Decide today.
It's the most important point: you decide today, calmly, what you'll do when you're scared.
Does it go in your Statement?
Your plan sets out **rules you control**. What goes in and what has no place there?
Goes in the plan
Doesn't belong
Allocation: 70 % global shares and 30 % bonds
The key decision, in writing.
I invest €200 on the 1st of every month
An automatic rule that depends on you.
The stock a TikToker recommended
A trend isn't a plan.
Where the IBEX will be in December
Nobody knows: predictions don't go in the plan.
I rebalance every January
When you go back to your allocation.
I'll never invest with borrowed money
It goes under «what I'll never do».
Sort the six sentences.
A good plan has **rules you control**: allocation, contributions, rebalancing and limits. No predictions, no trends.
Does it depend on you or on the market?
Sort each sentence
Bruno wants more
Bruno
My plan says 80 % shares and 20 % bonds.
But I've had two brilliant years. I'm switching to 100 % shares: bonds don't pay.
What do you tell him?
Go for it: the market's rising
Raising your risk after a rally is buying euphoria.
Reread why you chose 80/20. If your life hasn't changed, stick with it
Nice! The plan exists so you don't decide on the emotion of the moment.
Move it all into bonds, just in case
Switching out of fear isn't following the plan either.
Review it every year or if your life changes. **Never** because of the market.

steps.title: The template
steps.body:
1. Goals («X € in year Y for Z»).
2. Horizon.
3. Cushion.
4. Allocation.
5. Products and maximum cost.
6. Automatic contribution.
7. When I rebalance.
8. What I'll do if the market falls 30 %.
9. What I'll never do.
10. Speculation limit (optional).
steps.key: A plan written in a moment of calm is what saves you in a moment of panic.
steps.tip: Try it: set an alert 20 % below your main ETF; if it goes off, reread your plan.

steps.title: The challenge
steps.body:
You have **€10,000** to invest over 20 years (your cushion is already set aside). Build a portfolio that's diversified, cheap and that you can defend through a rough patch.

Use everything from this section: allocation based on horizon, several countries, few products, low costs and a small slice for speculation if you want.

steps.title: How to defend a portfolio
steps.body: With arguments, not predictions: «I own thousands of companies from all over the world, 20 % in bonds for the falls, a 0.2 % cost and a written rule for rebalancing». It's an exercise for learning, not a recommendation.
steps.key: A good portfolio isn't the one that rises most in a year, but the one you can stick with for 20 years.
steps.tip: Try it: build your portfolio in Market with virtual money, for example with VWCE and IEAG.

u30l7.title: When to sell (and when not to)

texts: «I'll just sell it»
Marta
My index fund has fallen **15 %** in two months. I'm selling before it falls further.
Before you sell, one question: why did you buy it?
To retire, 25 years from now.
Has any of that changed?
Yes: the price has gone down
The price wasn't your reason. Your reason was having that money 25 years from now.
No: I still won't need that money for 25 years
Then nothing that matters has changed. Only today's price.
I don't know, but I'd rather not risk it
That's human. Which is why it helps to decide **beforehand** what would make you sell.
You sell when **your life** or **your plan** changes. Hardly ever because the price has.
Is it a reason to sell?
Six situations for someone investing for the long term. Separate the **real reasons** from the ones that are just noise.
Could be a reason
Not a reason
In two years you'll need the money for a deposit on a flat
Your time horizon has shortened: time to lower the risk little by little.
The stock market has fallen 20 % this month
A fall is part of the journey. If you don't need the money, it doesn't change your plan.
Shares make up 85 % and your plan says 70 %
That's rebalancing: you sell the excess to get back to your allocation.
A headline announces «the worst crisis in decades»
Headlines don't call the bottom or the top.
You bought a company for its business and that business no longer exists
Your reason for holding it has gone: the thesis is broken.
Your fund is up 30 % and «you should lock it in»
Having risen says nothing about what it will do. Your plan never mentioned a price.
Sort the six situations.
The three real reasons: **you need the money**, **it's time to rebalance** or **the reason you bought is broken**. Today's price, on its own, is none of the three.
Has your life changed, your plan, or only the price?
Sort each situation
The reason you bought
Bruno
I bought shares in a chain of shops because it was opening stores and earning more every year.
Now it's closing shops, losing money and owing more and more. But I'm down 40 %: I'll wait to get it back.
What do you tell him?
To wait: if he sells, the loss becomes real
The loss is already real. The question is whether he'd buy it again today.
To ask himself whether he'd buy it today, knowing what he knows
That's the question. If the answer is no, his reason for holding it no longer exists.
To buy more to lower his average price
That's putting more money into a reason that no longer stands up.
That's called a **broken thesis**. With a fund holding thousands of companies it hardly ever happens; with a single share, it does.
Selling has costs too: commissions and, if there's a gain, tax. Between investment funds in Spain you can transfer without paying tax.

steps.title: Three reasons, and one that isn't
steps.body:
**Reasons to sell:**

• **You need the money** or your goal is close: lower the risk little by little, not all at once.
• **Rebalancing**: you go back to your plan's allocation.
• **Broken thesis**: the reason you bought has gone.

**Not a reason:** the price having gone up or down, a headline or what someone else says.

Before selling, ask yourself: «if I didn't own it today, would I buy it?».
steps.key: You sell because of what has changed in your life or your plan, not because of what the price has done.
steps.tip: Try it: open your Portfolio and write in the journal, for each position, what would have to happen for you to sell it.

u30l8.title: How much do I need to retire? The 4 % rule

texts: A number to start with
Elena
I want to know how much I'd need saved to stop working. Is there a sum for that?
There's a widely used one: the **4 % rule**. Work out what you'd spend a year from your savings and **multiply it by 25**.
Elena would need €20,000 a year from her savings, on top of her pension. What capital does that give?
That's ten years of spending. The rule multiplies by 25.
That's multiplying by 4. The rule says you withdraw 4 %, not that four years is enough.
It's the same sum seen the other way round: having **25 times** your spending means being able to withdraw **4 %** a year.
What the rule doesn't say
Bruno
So with €500,000 that's it: I take out €20,000 every year and the money **never runs out**.
Is that so?
Yes: that's why it's called a rule
It's a rule of thumb for doing the numbers, not a law. Nobody guarantees the future.
No: it came from past data and retirements of about 30 years
That's it. It was worked out with US shares and bonds from the last century, for about 30 years.
Yes, if he has it all in shares
All in shares makes the ride rougher, not safer.
It doesn't count **taxes or fees** either. And if you retire very young, 30 years falls short.
It's useful for an order of magnitude. After that, what you control matters most: **how much you spend**, when you start saving and your pension.

steps.title: The 4 % rule, with its limits
steps.body:
**The sum:** what you need a year from your savings × 25. Or the other way round: of whatever you have, 4 % a year.

**Where it comes from:** studies using US data (Bengen, 1994) for retirements of about 30 years.

**Its limits:**

• It isn't a guarantee: the future may differ from the past.
• For more than 30 years you need to be more cautious.
• It doesn't deduct taxes or fees.

Use it to see roughly where your number lies, and review it every few years.
steps.key: Twenty-five times your annual spending is a starting point, not a promise.
steps.tip: Try it: work out a year of your spending, multiply it by 25 and note the figure in your journal.

texts: Eighteen years ahead
Laura
My daughter has just been born. I want to set aside **€50 a month** for when she turns 18.
I'll put it in a no-risk account: you don't gamble with children.
What's special about this money?
That it can never lose: everything risk-free
No stock market risk, true. But over 18 years inflation eats a large part of it.
That it has 18 years ahead of it
That's it. With that much time it can hold quite a lot in shares: there's time to recover from falls.
That it should go into whatever rises most
Chasing what rises most is betting. The usual rule applies here too: diversified and cheap.
And when there are only a few years left before it's needed, you lower the risk little by little. As with any goal.
In whose name?
Pablo
I'm going to open a fund for my son. Do I put it in his name or mine?
They're two different paths, and it's worth choosing knowing what changes.
If he puts it in his son's name, what changes?
Nothing: the father always runs it just the same
He manages it while his son is a minor. But the money is no longer his.
The money is the son's: at 18 he decides
That's it. And the father can't take it back for himself, even if he needs it.
It earns more
The fund is the same. What changes is whose it is, not how much it makes.
In the father's name, he controls it and hands it over when he likes. Neither option is better: it depends on what you're after.
Putting money in a child's name is a gift. Find out how it's declared in your region before doing it.

steps.title: A plan for a child
steps.body:
• **What for and for when**: studies, a first car, a boost at 18.
• **Long horizon**: with many years ahead there's room for quite a lot in shares, diversified and cheap.
• **A little, but every month**: €50 a month for 18 years at 5 % a year (an example, not a promise) comes to about **€17,460**, of which €10,800 is what you put in.
• **In whose name**: the child's (it's theirs, and at 18 they decide) or yours (you control it).
• **As the date gets close**, lower the risk.

What's worth most isn't the money: it's your child understanding how it was built.
steps.key: For a child, the long horizon is the advantage. And deciding in whose name is the question not to skip.
steps.tip: Try it: in Market, look at how much a global ETF has risen in recent years and think about what horizon your goal would have.

u30l1-1.prompt: Your plan is 60/40 and after a good run you're at 72/28. Rebalancing means…
options: Buying more shares, since they're doing well
u30l1-1.explanation: You go back to the level of risk you chose when you were calm.

u30l1-5.prompt: Your portfolio has drifted to 75 % shares and 25 % fixed income. Your plan is 60/40. Allocate how it should end up: between 58 % and 62 % in shares.
options: Global bond fund hedged to euros
u30l1-5.explanation: Going back to 60/40 returns the portfolio to the risk you decided on. Educational example, not a recommendation.

u30l1-6.prompt: Match each way of rebalancing with how it works.
u30l1-6.explanation: All three work; with contributions you avoid selling and paying tax.
right: You correct if one part drifts more than 5 points
You review on a fixed date, for example every January
New money goes to whatever has fallen behind

u30l1-9.prompt: If you decide to correct only when one part drifts more than 5 points, you're rebalancing by ____.
u30l1-9.explanation: You can also do it by calendar, once a year.

u30l1-10.prompt: With investment funds in Spain, how can you rebalance without paying tax?
options: By selling and buying on the same day
u30l1-10.explanation: A transfer between funds isn't taxed until you finally cash out. ETFs don't have this advantage.

u30l1-11.prompt: Your plan is 70 % shares and 30 % bonds, and after a good year you're at 78/22. This month you're putting in €300. What do you do?
options: I sell all the extra shares right now
I put the €300 into shares, since they're the ones doing well
u30l1-11.explanation: Rebalancing with your contributions brings the portfolio back to your plan without selling, so you trigger no tax. Putting the money into whatever is rising most seems logical, but it takes you away from the risk you chose.
feedback: Good! You rebalance without selling anything, so you pay no tax.
It works, but if they're ETFs or shares, selling at a gain is taxed. With contributions you avoid that.
That takes you even further from the plan: more and more risk than you chose.

u30l2-3.prompt: Putting in €300 a month for 30 years, how much separates 0.2 % in costs from 1.8 %?
u30l2-3.explanation: About €338,200 versus about €253,400 with the market at 7 %: almost €85,000 of difference.

u30l2-5.prompt: Which costs should you check before investing? Select all that apply.
options: The commission on buying and selling
The fund's ongoing charges or TER
u30l2-5.explanation: The trading commission and the ongoing charges (TER); also currency exchange, the spread, custody fees and taxes. Past returns or the broker's size aren't costs.

u30l2-10.prompt: Lumi's fund charges 1.5 %, but it rose 10 % this year, and she thinks the cost doesn't matter. What do you reply?
options: Then better a fund that charges 3 %
u30l2-10.explanation: Judge a fund against its index and over many years, not on one good year.
feedback: That 10 % is already net of fees, but without them it would have been 11.5 %. And in a year it doesn't rise, you still pay the 1.5 %.
That's it! What matters is how much it leaves you compared with the cheap alternative, year after year.
Charging more doesn't make it rise more. The only sure thing about a fee is that you pay it.
lines: My fund charges 1.5 %, but it's up 10 % this year 🚀
So the cost doesn't matter, right?

u30l2-11.prompt: You have an MSCI World ETF that charges 0.20 %, with good gains. You find another on the same index at 0.12 %. What do you do?
options: I don't care: costs don't matter
I keep the one I have and send new contributions to the cheap one
I sell mine now and buy the cheap one with the lot
u30l2-11.explanation: Between two cheap ETFs on the same index, the difference is small and selling has a certain tax cost. The sensible thing is for new money to go to the cheaper one. Switching all at once only pays off when the gap is big, like from 1.5 % to 0.2 %.
feedback: They do matter, but here the difference is small. What would be costly is selling in a hurry.
That's it! You save costs on the new money without paying tax for selling the old.
Selling an ETF at a gain is taxed today: you'd pay tax to save 0.08 % a year.

u30l3-5.prompt: You split your €50 a month. Rules: at least 2 products, none above 85 %, at most 5 % in crypto and 10 % in a single share.
u30l3-5.explanation: The core, diversified and cheap; the speculative part, small. Crypto is very volatile and you can lose everything you put in. An example, not a recommendation.

u30l3-7.prompt: If every €50 purchase costs you €2 in fees, you lose 4 % straight away.
u30l3-7.explanation: 2 ÷ 50 = 4 %. With little money, look for options with no fixed fee per purchase.

u30l3-9.prompt: Quick: with a large lump sum, what came out ahead more often in Vanguard's studies?
u30l3-9.explanation: About two times out of three, because the market rises more often than it falls. With a salary, investing every month is the natural thing to do.

u30l3-10.prompt: Lumi can only save €50 a month and thinks that won't get her anywhere. What do you reply?
options: Start with €50 and raise it when you earn more: time does the rest
You're right, better to spend it
Wait until you can invest €500 a month, then it'll count
u30l3-10.explanation: A little, started early, goes a long way. What matters is the habit.
feedback: That's the way! What counts most is starting early and not stopping.
Spending is fine, but €50 a month over decades can turn into tens of thousands of euros.
Waiting until you «have more» usually means never starting: what counts most is time.
lines: I can only save €50 a month 😔
I won't get anywhere with that, will I?

u30l3-11.prompt: You put €50 a month into an index fund. This month the stock market has fallen 20 %. What do you do with the contribution?
options: I keep it: I buy cheaper
I sell what I have so I don't lose more
I pause it until the market recovers
u30l3-11.explanation: With a fixed contribution, when the price falls you buy more units and your average price falls. Pausing in the dips seems prudent, but it means you stop buying just when it's cheapest.
feedback: That's it! Contributing in the dips lowers your average price without you having to guess anything.
Selling in the fall turns a temporary drop into a permanent loss.
You stop buying just when it's cheap: you miss the units at a better price.

u30l3-12.prompt: You're going to invest €50 a month. Broker A charges €3 per purchase and its ETF 0.10 % a year. Broker B charges nothing to buy and its ETF costs 0.20 %. Which suits you?
options: B: no charge on each purchase
It doesn't matter: the difference is tiny
u30l3-12.explanation: With little money, a fixed fee eats a chunk of every contribution (€3 out of €50 is far more than a tenth of a point a year). That's why the cheapest ETF isn't always the cheapest option.
feedback: Its ETF is, but €3 of every €50 goes before it's invested: that weighs far more.
Exactly. With small contributions, a fixed fee per purchase is the most expensive thing.
It isn't: with €50 a month, €3 per purchase takes a big part of every contribution.

u30l4-3.prompt: An investment doubles in value (+100 %) over 10 years. Its annualised return is…?
u30l4-3.explanation: 2^(1/10) − 1 ≈ 7.2 %. It fits the rule of 72: 72 ÷ 7.2 = 10 years.

u30l4-4.prompt: The return that measures what the fund did, regardless of when you put money in, is the ____-weighted return.
u30l4-4.explanation: It's the one used to compare funds and managers with each other.

u30l4-5.prompt: Match each measure with its use.
u30l4-5.explanation: Each one answers a different question.
right: How much the value has changed in total

u30l4-9.prompt: An app boasts that your portfolio is «+40 % since you started». You started 7 years ago. A global index fund has returned 7 % a year over that time. How do you rate it?
options: Brilliant: 40 % is an awful lot of money
I annualise it: about 4.9 % a year
Better not to look at the return
u30l4-9.explanation: A total figure without a timeframe says nothing. Annualise it and compare with a benchmark index.
feedback: Without the timeframe you can't tell: over 7 years, 40 % is less than 5 % a year.
Exactly. Only by annualising can you compare, and here the comparison doesn't come out well.
Measuring properly is exactly what lets you make decisions.

u30l4-10.prompt: What should you take into account to measure your return honestly? Select all that apply.
options: Compare it with a benchmark index
Look only at your best year
Count only the investments that won
u30l4-10.explanation: What counts is the result net of fees and taxes, after inflation and against an index. Looking at your best year or only at what won tells a nicer story than the real one.

u30l4-11.prompt: Fund A advertises «+60 % in 10 years». Fund B, «6 % a year over the last 5 years». Which did better each year?
options: B: A is under 5 % a year
u30l4-11.explanation: To compare, everything has to be in % a year. 60 divided by 10 would be 6 %, but because it compounds you need less each year to reach 60 %, so A is behind B.
feedback: You're comparing a total with a yearly pace. You have to put them in the same measure.
Good! Spread over 10 years and compounded, that 60 % gives less than B's 6 % a year.
You can: by annualising both. And careful, different periods don't tell you what happens next.

u30l5-1.prompt: Put the first sections of an Investment Policy Statement in order.
u30l5-1.explanation: First what and by when; then with what emergency fund, how to allocate and with which products.

u30l5-2.prompt: You review the Statement once a year or when your ____ changes, not when the market changes.
u30l5-2.explanation: A new job or a child changes your goals; a stock market fall doesn't.

u30l5-3.prompt: Which point in the Statement protects you most from panic?
u30l5-3.explanation: You decide it calmly and remind yourself of it when everyone is selling.

u30l5-4.prompt: What can go in the «what I'll never do» section? Select all that apply.
options: Review the portfolio once a year
u30l5-4.explanation: «Never» is for what hurts you: buying what you don't understand, investing with borrowed money or concentrating too much in a single asset. Contributing every month and reviewing once a year are part of the plan.

u30l5-12.prompt: Your Statement says «in the speculative part, always with a stop». You buy bitcoin at the last price. Place the stop a little below the recent low.
u30l5-12.explanation: The written rule decides how much you can lose before fear or euphoria decide for you. The stop goes a little below the recent low: right on top of it, any wick would trigger it.

u30l6-1.prompt: Allocate the €10,000. Rules: at least 4 products, none above 60 %, at least 15 % in bonds, at most 10 % in gold, 10 % in a single share and 5 % in crypto.
options: Global bond fund hedged to euros
u30l6-1.explanation: A diversified, cheap core, a cushion of bonds for the falls and the speculative part kept limited. You can lose everything in crypto. Educational example, not a recommendation.

u30l6-2.prompt: You've set aside a small slice for speculation. You want to trade the IBEX 35 without risking more than 1 % of your €10,000 (€100). Choose the amount and place the stop.
u30l6-2.explanation: The speculative part has rules too: the stop and the size decide how much you can lose, not the market.

u30l6-3.prompt: Year one: the stock market falls 25 % and your portfolio 18 %. A friend tells you to sell everything. What do you do?
options: Move it all into a deposit until things calm down
Follow the plan: contribute, rebalance into shares if needed and don't sell
u30l6-3.explanation: Bonds cushioned the fall (−18 % versus −25 %). Now it's time for point 8 of your plan.
feedback: Getting out «until things calm down» is selling low: nobody tells you when to return, and rebounds come without warning.
Good: with a 20-year horizon, a bad year is part of the journey.
Turning a fall into a permanent loss is the most expensive mistake in market history.

u30l6-4.prompt: A colleague tells you: «Sell the bonds and put everything into the share that's risen most this year». What do you reply?
options: That my allocation is for 20 years
That I'll think about it if it rises another 20 %
I take their advice: bonds don't earn anything
u30l6-4.explanation: Diversifying means giving up on picking the star of the year in exchange for not depending on it.
feedback: That's how you defend a portfolio: with the plan, not with the latest headline.
Waiting for it to rise further before getting in is the same mistake, just later.
Bonds are there for the falls, not to earn more. And chasing whatever rose most usually arrives late.

u30l6-5.prompt: Which argument best defends a diversified portfolio?
options: «An influencer says it's going to go up»
«Last year it rose more than my cousin's»
u30l6-5.explanation: Diversification, cost and tolerance for falls: the things you can control.

u30l6-7.prompt: What should your €10,000 portfolio over 20 years have? Select all that apply.
options: A change of funds every few months
A big bet on the latest trend
u30l6-7.explanation: Low costs and diversification across companies and countries, with a rule for rebalancing. Changing funds every few months or betting big on the latest trend works against that; the speculative part, if there is one, small and limited.

u30l6-9.prompt: Put the steps for getting your portfolio up and running in order.
options: Have your emergency fund set aside
u30l6-9.explanation: First the foundation and the key decision; then the products and the discipline.

u30l6-10.prompt: Lumi asks you to defend your portfolio: why do you think it will work? What do you reply?
options: Because the stock market always goes up if you wait long enough
It's diversified and I know what I'll do in a fall
Because I've picked whatever will rise most
u30l6-10.explanation: You defend a portfolio with diversification, costs and a plan, not with predictions.
feedback: Over the long term it has gone up, but with falls of up to 50 % along the way.
Perfect defence! You talked about what you control, not what you're guessing.
Nobody knows what will rise most. A portfolio that depends on guessing right is fragile.
lines: Go on then, defend your portfolio 🧐
Why do you think it's going to work?

u30l2-12.prompt: You buy €2,000 of an ETF that trades in dollars and your broker charges 0.5 % for currency conversion. How much do you pay for the conversion when you buy?
u30l2-12.explanation: 2,000 × 0.005 = €10. When you sell you'll pay the conversion again.

u30l2-13.prompt: Is it a cost of the product or of your broker?
u30l2-13.explanation: The product's costs are in the KID cost table; the broker's are on its fees page. You have to add both.

u30l2-14.prompt: Your broker doesn't charge for buying, but it does charge €2 a month for custody. You have €600 invested. What percentage of your investment does it cost you per year?
u30l2-14.explanation: 2 × 12 = €24 a year; 24 ÷ 600 = 0.04 → 4 %. With little money, a fixed fee eats up the return.

u30l2-15.prompt: Match each line of the KID cost table with what it is.
u30l2-15.explanation: The «Composition of costs» table is the same in every KID, so you can compare two products line by line.
right: An extra if the fund beats a target
What the fund spends moving its holdings
What you pay when you buy

u30l2-16.prompt: If a broker advertises «€0 commission», buying with it costs nothing.
u30l2-16.explanation: It may charge for currency conversion, for custody or through the price at which it executes your order. Check the full fee schedule.

u30l3-13.prompt: You put in €50 a month and pay €3 per purchase. If you make a single €150 purchase every three months, what percentage does the commission take?
u30l3-13.explanation: 3 ÷ 150 = 0.02 → 2 %, instead of the 6 % of buying every month.

u30l3-14.prompt: You have €400 invested and your bank charges you €20 a year for custody. What do you do?
options: I sell and leave it in my current account
I look for a broker or platform with no custody fee
feedback: You stop investing over a cost you can avoid by switching provider.
That's it: with little money, removing a fixed cost is worth more than fine-tuning the product.
On €400 that's 5 % every year, win or lose.
u30l3-14.explanation: A fixed cost is measured against your amount: €20 on €400 is 5 %; on €40,000, it's 0.05 %.

u30l7-1.prompt: Could it be a reason to sell?
options: Shares weigh more than your plan says
You need the money in two years
The stock market has fallen 20 % this month
The reason you bought no longer exists
u30l7-1.explanation: Your life, your plan or your thesis can be a reason. Today's price or a headline can't.

u30l7-2.prompt: Ana has €20,000 in a global equity fund. In two years she'll need it for a deposit on a flat. The stock market is at record highs. What does she do?
options: Waits for it to fall a little to sell better
Leaves it all: the market is doing great
Gradually moves the money into something low-risk
feedback: Waiting for a fall in order to sell is betting on exactly what would hurt her.
In two years a sharp fall would leave her without a deposit. Her horizon is no longer long.
Good: the reason isn't the price, it's that her time horizon has shortened.
u30l7-2.explanation: When the goal gets close, you lower the risk little by little. It has nothing to do with whether the market is high or low.

options: An analyst has lowered their recommendation
The reason you bought no longer exists
The share has fallen more than 20 %
u30l7-3.explanation: The thesis is your reason for holding something. If that reason goes, holding on is just waiting.

u30l7-4.prompt: If your fund has risen a lot, the sensible thing is to sell to lock in the gain.
u30l7-4.explanation: Having risen says nothing about what it will do next. You sell if you need it, if it's time to rebalance or if your plan said so.

u30l7-5.prompt: Your plan is 70 % shares and 30 % bonds. Your portfolio is worth €10,000 and shares make up 80 %. How many euros of shares do you sell to get back to the plan?
u30l7-5.explanation: You have €8,000 in shares and your plan says €7,000: you sell €1,000 and move it into bonds.

u30l7-6.prompt: Put in order what to ask yourself before selling.
u30l7-6.explanation: First the reason and whether it still stands; then the plan and the costs. The decision comes at the end, not the beginning.

u30l7-7.prompt: Which are reasonable grounds for selling? Tick all that apply.
options: The price has fallen and you're scared
Your goal is two years away
You're going back to your plan's allocation
u30l7-7.explanation: Rebalancing and getting close to your goal are reasons. Fear of a fall or what someone else does doesn't change your plan.

lines: My index fund has gone a year without rising 😒
I'll sell it and find one that does better, right?
u30l7-8.prompt: Lumi's index fund has gone a year without rising and she wants to sell it to find one that does better. What do you reply?
options: Yes: a whole year without rising is a bad sign
Has your horizon or your plan changed? If not, a year isn't a reason
Sell half and try another one
feedback: A flat year is normal in the stock market. Switching funds over that is chasing what has already risen.
Exactly! The fund is still what you bought. What has changed is your patience.
Selling half out of impatience is the same mistake, by halves.
u30l7-8.explanation: A year without rising doesn't break any thesis or change your horizon. Switching to the fund that rose most last year usually works out expensive.

u30l7-9.prompt: Before selling, ask yourself: «if I didn't own it today, would I ____ it?».
u30l7-9.explanation: If the answer is yes, there's no reason to sell. If it's no, ask yourself why you still hold it.

u30l8-1.prompt: You reckon you'd need €24,000 a year from your savings. According to the 4 % rule, what capital would you need?

u30l8-2.prompt: You have €300,000 saved. According to the 4 % rule, how many euros could you withdraw in the first year?

u30l8-3.prompt: The 4 % rule guarantees your savings will never run out.
u30l8-3.explanation: It's a rule of thumb for doing the numbers with past data. It guarantees nothing.

u30l8-4.prompt: What limits does the 4 % rule have? Tick all that apply.
options: It only works for crypto investors
It forces you to sell everything when you retire
It was worked out for about 30 years of retirement
It comes from past US data
u30l8-4.explanation: It comes from past US data and retirements of about 30 years; it also doesn't deduct taxes or fees. It says nothing about crypto and doesn't force you to sell anything.

u30l8-5.prompt: Marta is 30 and wants to stop working at 45. She does her sums with the 4 % rule. What would you tell her?
options: It works as it is: that's the rule
Be more cautious: her retirement would last much longer than 30 years
u30l8-5.explanation: The more years the money has to last, the more cautious you need to be about what you withdraw.
feedback: Without a number she doesn't know whether she's on track. The rule works as a starting point.
The rule was worked out for about 30 years of retirement. Hers could last 50.
Good: with more years ahead you need more capital, or to withdraw less each year.

u30l8-6.prompt: Put the steps for working out your number in order.
options: Subtract what your pension will cover
Work out a year of your spending
u30l8-6.explanation: First how much you spend; then what share your savings will have to cover; and the figure gets reviewed, because your life changes.

u30l8-7.prompt: Lumi has read that you need a million euros to retire and thinks she'll never get there. What do you reply?
options: It depends on what you spend: do your own sums
It's true: no million, no retirement
u30l8-7.explanation: Each person's figure comes from their annual spending and what their pension covers. A headline knows neither.
feedback: Exactly! Your number comes from your spending and your pension, not from a headline.
There's no single figure for everyone: it depends on what each person spends.
Every euro saved brings your number closer, whatever it is.
lines: I've read you need a million euros to retire 😩

u30l8-8.prompt: Having 25 times your annual spending is the same as withdrawing ____ % a year.

u30l8-9.prompt: Of everything that affects your number, what weighs most and is up to you?
options: How much you spend a year
u30l8-9.explanation: Every euro less of annual spending is 25 euros less of capital needed.

u30l9-1.prompt: You contribute €50 a month for 18 years. How much money have you put in yourself in total?
u30l9-1.explanation: 50 × 12 × 18 = €10,800. The rest, if any, is whatever it has earned.

u30l9-2.prompt: For a newborn, the most prudent thing is to leave the money for 18 years in an account paying no interest.
u30l9-2.explanation: Over 18 years inflation takes away a large part of its value. Such a long horizon allows for some risk.

u30l9-3.prompt: Which option does it belong to?
options: You can use it yourself if you need it
You decide when to hand it over
You can't take it back for yourself
u30l9-3.explanation: In their name, the money is theirs. In yours, you keep deciding.

u30l9-4.prompt: Laura's daughter turns 16. In two years she'll use the money for her studies, and it's all in an equity fund. What does Laura do?
options: Waits until the last month to sell it all
Leaves it: it has done very well for 16 years
Gradually moves the money into something low-risk
u30l9-4.explanation: The same money that could go into shares with an 18-year horizon no longer can with two years to go.
feedback: Staking everything on a single day's price is the biggest risk she could take.
In two years a sharp fall would leave the money short just when it's needed.
Good: the horizon is no longer long, so the risk comes down little by little.

u30l9-5.prompt: Why can savings for a newborn hold quite a lot in shares?
options: Because it has many years to recover from falls
Because the stock market rises more for them
u30l9-5.explanation: What allows you to take risk is the time horizon, not the age of whoever will receive it.

u30l9-6.prompt: Put the steps of a plan for a child in order.
options: Choose whose name it goes in
Lower the risk as the date gets close
Decide what for and for when
u30l9-6.explanation: First the goal and whose money it will be; then consistency; and finally, protecting what has been built.

u30l9-7.prompt: Lumi has opened an account paying no interest for her grandson for when he turns 18. What do you reply?
options: Over 18 years inflation eats part of it: look at options that beat it
Better buy him the trendy share
u30l9-7.explanation: Eighteen years is a very long horizon. Leaving the money idle isn't avoiding risk: it's a certain loss of purchasing power.
feedback: Exactly! With that much time it can afford something more than an account.
A single share is a bet, not an 18-year plan.
With no interest, in 18 years that money will buy quite a bit less.
lines: I've opened an account with no interest for my grandson 👶
That way his money will be safe when he turns 18.

u30l9-8.prompt: What helps in an 18-year plan? Tick all that apply.
options: Waiting until you have a large amount
Contributing a little, but every month
u30l9-8.explanation: Consistency and low costs work in your favour over 18 years. Switching funds every year or waiting until you «have more» works against you.

u30l9-9.prompt: When there are only a few years left before the money is needed, it's time to lower the ____.
u30l9-9.explanation: With little time ahead there's no room to recover from a fall.
